Gastroenterology · published research

Radiation-induced enteropathy

Summary of the Evidence

One 2019 publication combined cell-culture experiments using human umbilical-cord-blood mesenchymal stem cells with a mouse model of radiation-induced enteropathy. PBM preconditioned the stem cells before administration; the intestine itself was not directly illuminated. The cell and mouse findings are parts of one experimental programme (Kim et al. 2019).

Human and clinical evidence

No clinical study in people receiving abdominal radiotherapy was identified. Laboratory work with human-derived cells does not show how patients respond to treatment.

Animal evidence

After a single whole-abdominal X-ray dose of 13.5 Gy, mice received intravenous PBM-preconditioned stem cells, untreated stem cells, or vehicle, in two injections two days apart. Compared with the control groups, the PBM-preconditioned-cell group had less mucosal destruction, greater crypt-cell proliferation and epithelial-barrier function, less loss of intestinal microvascular endothelial cells, and more angiogenesis in the lamina propria. These are tissue outcomes in an acute mouse model, not patient outcomes (Kim et al. 2019).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

In cultured human stem cells, 633-nm red visible light at 1 J/cm² increased proliferation and self-renewal. Conditioned medium from the treated cells reduced radiation-related endothelial-cell apoptosis and impaired tube formation, alongside higher levels of angiogenic factors. These findings support the cell-conditioning mechanism tested in mice but do not show an effect of PBM alone on intestinal tissue (Kim et al. 2019).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Cell experiments used 633-nm red light, with an irradiance of 7.12 mW/cm² and a fluence of 1 J/cm² selected for the main experiments. In mice, cells were given intravenously twice after whole-abdominal irradiation, two days apart. PBM was applied to the cells before infusion, not to the bowel. The study did not compare clinical delivery routes or a range of conditioning doses (Kim et al. 2019).

Interpretation

The publication reports improved intestinal barrier, crypt, endothelial, and angiogenesis measures after PBM-preconditioned cells were administered to irradiated mice. It supports a preclinical cell-conditioning strategy, but does not establish that PBM alone treats radiation enteropathy or improves outcomes for patients.

Publications and records

1 publication

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Very low for intestinal tissue outcomes after PBM-preconditioned cell therapy in irradiated mice

The finding comes from one preclinical publication (Kim et al. 2019).

Rationale for the certainty assessment

The evidence is one publication with cell-culture and mouse components. The improved tissue measures follow combined cell therapy and PBM preconditioning, so they do not establish the effect of PBM alone. No patient study or independent animal replication was identified (Kim et al. 2019).
